newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - Wheat strong, AWB ships lots.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - Wheat strong, AWB ships lots.

text.p: New signs of a significant upturn in grain prices are joining Australia's record wheat shipment performance as the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) is deluged with criticism and praise.

Last week the AWB shipped a further 229,037 tonnes of wheat, bringing its shipments to 8.35 million tonnes so far this shipping year, far ahead of the 5.81 million tonnes shipped in the same period of the previous year.
Shipment records are tumbling every month.
January set a new record of 2.1 million tonnes, the short month of February raised the record to 2.24 million tonnes, and March looks like beating the record again.
The AWB's main critic, the United States, is a rival which AWB executives lose few opportunities to say has been beaten on world markets this season.

U.S. criticism that the AWB, through its monopoly export powers, is a manipulative anti-free trade force in world wheat, is joined by cautious criticism in Australia by private traders that the board's monopoly power marginalises them in the market.

The AWB's supporters point to the board as a model of one Australian industry which handles export markets well. The fragmented Australian coal industry, where many sellers compete against each other in a unified Japanese market, is held up as the model which the AWB's monopoly avoids.

All of the main streams in the AWB debate came together in the past week as Australian wheat exports surged, prices looked like rising again and as antagonistic factions in Australia's grains industry finally agreed on a new commercialised structure for the board --- woven around retention of the export monopoly.

Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd pointed out on Friday that astonishment in December at the size of the Australian crop and consternation over how it would be sold had been replaced just months later with tight supply.

"(Now) nearly all the wheat is committed, the AWB is winning tenders all over the place on quality and price, we're shipping record amounts, everything's going flat out, we're doing very well," he said.
Booth believes a looming price upturn will be reinforced by wheat users quickly covering themselves when the break occurs.
Last year, the wheat price inched down when nobody believed it could fall, now it could inch up in a significant total gain.
Most feed grains were dearer in Australia last week, while Chicago's strong run on Thursday night is seen as further vindicating the AWB's stand in keeping pools prices high.
Last week cash Australian Standard White (ASW) rose by about A$2.00 a tonne to about A$175.00 Newcastle, while sorghum added A$3.00-A$5.00 to A$160.00 bid April/May and A$162.00 May/June.
This created new seasonal highs for sorghum and helped fuel an emerging debate about where the new crop stands.

Cameron Pratt of GrainCo said big yields presently being returned for sorghum suggested a crop of about 370,000 tonnes for New South Wales alone, far ahead of the officially-forecast 350,000 tonnes but less than the state's record of 490,000 tonnes in 1983/84, with 325,000 an average harvest.

Australia's sorghum harvest is getting underway with the national 1996/97 crop officially forecast at 1.1 million tonnes. Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders, however, said the sorghum crop was "the big unknown".
Yields were very good where the crop was undamaged by recent heavy rain, but the full state of the crop would not be known until April, he said.
Australian wheat futures showed signs of rising on Friday with settlement prices for more distant contracts moving ahead.
Near-term settlement pricesd over the week were mostly steady while prices for more distant contracts rose by A$4.00-A$5.00 a tonne.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
